authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — unreviewed candidate generation

items.prompt: A monitoring system must report the maximum total load over every contiguous block of exactly 7 days. Which property is the decisive sliding-window signal?
constraints: The block must contain exactly 7 adjacent days.
Only the maximum total is required.

options.text: Successive candidates overlap and differ by one outgoing value and one incoming value.
The prompt asks for a maximum.
The input values are numeric.
Any solution can name a left and a right index.

feedback.reason: The decisive signal is a fixed-length contiguous candidate whose state can be updated by removing one value and adding one value.

blocks.text: A window is justified by structure, not by the word ‘maximum’. Every legal candidate is a length-7 interval, and moving from days [l..r] to [l+1..r+1] preserves six of seven values. A running sum therefore changes by subtracting the outgoing load and adding the incoming load. Numeric input alone and the existence of two indices do not establish a window invariant. This reasoning transfers to any fixed-length aggregate, including averages, counts, and frequency summaries; it does not require values to be positive because no monotonic shrink rule is used.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.maximum_word: Many non-window problems ask for a maximum. The missing requirement is overlapping contiguous candidates with incrementally maintainable state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.numeric_input: Numeric values permit arithmetic but do not determine the traversal. Non-contiguous, prefix-based, or dynamic-programming problems can also be numeric.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_indices: Two indices are an implementation detail. They become a sliding window only when they delimit a maintained contiguous candidate with a legal movement rule.

items.prompt: Choose any set of positions, not necessarily adjacent, so that no two chosen positions are consecutive and the chosen values have maximum total. Which classification is correct?
constraints: Chosen positions may be separated by arbitrary gaps.
No two chosen positions may be adjacent.

options.text: Use a fixed window of length 2 because adjacency is mentioned.
Use a variable window and shrink whenever two chosen positions become adjacent.
This is not a sliding-window objective because a candidate is not one contiguous interval; state must compare take/skip choices.
Use a frequency-constrained window keyed by position parity.

feedback.reason: A sliding window represents one contiguous range; this objective selects a non-contiguous subset and requires take/skip state.

blocks.text: The output contract is the decisive boundary. A candidate solution may include positions 0, 3, and 7 while excluding the values between them, so no pair of moving boundaries encloses exactly the selected state. A fixed or variable window would force every position between left and right into the candidate. The appropriate reasoning is dynamic: at each position compare the best total that skips it with the best earlier compatible total plus its value. This near miss prevents the shallow rule ‘array plus adjacency language means window’.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_window_two: A length-2 interval only inspects neighbouring pairs; it cannot represent a globally optimal set containing several separated positions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_window: Shrinking a contiguous range cannot encode arbitrary take/skip choices inside that range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.frequency_window: Position parity does not express the no-adjacent selection constraint, and a frequency map still describes all elements inside a contiguous range.

items.prompt: Task A asks for the maximum average of exactly k consecutive readings. Task B asks for the longest consecutive segment containing at most k distinct labels. Which classification is correct?
constraints: Both tasks require a contiguous segment.
Task A fixes length; Task B fixes a validity condition.

options.text: Both use fixed-size windows because each statement contains k.
Task A uses a fixed-size window; Task B uses a variable-size frequency-constrained window.
Both use variable-size windows because both optimize an answer.
Task A uses a variable-size window; Task B uses a fixed-size window.

feedback.reason: In Task A, k is the required length; in Task B, k bounds a maintained property while length is the answer.

blocks.text: The same symbol can play different roles. ‘Exactly k consecutive readings’ fixes the distance between the boundaries, so every legal candidate has the same size. ‘At most k distinct labels’ allows many lengths; expansion adds a label and the left boundary moves only when the distinct-count invariant is violated. The decision is based on whether k constrains size or validity, not on the presence of k itself. This distinction transfers to budgets, duplicate limits, and other at-most constraints.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_fixed: Task B can have any length from zero upward; k limits distinct labels, not the number of elements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_variable: Task A has no validity repair loop. Its legal size is predetermined and does not vary with the data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.a_variable_b_fixed: This reverses the roles of k: Task A fixes size, whereas Task B fixes a property of a variable-length range.

items.prompt: A log analyzer needs the longest contiguous run containing at most three distinct event types. Which signal best identifies the intended pattern?
constraints: The run must be contiguous.
Length is maximized subject to an at-most-three-distinct validity rule.

options.text: Sort all events so equal types become adjacent.
Use a fixed window of length three.
Use one numeric prefix sum over event identifiers.
Maintain event frequencies, expand right, and move left only while the distinct-count limit is violated.

feedback.reason: Contiguity, a local frequency constraint, and a longest-valid objective point to a variable frequency-constrained window.

blocks.text: The maintained object is the current contiguous run. Adding the next event changes one frequency; if the number of distinct keys exceeds three, advancing left can restore validity while preserving every possible longer ending at the current right boundary. Sorting would destroy original contiguity, a length-three window confuses the limit with size, and a scalar prefix total cannot recover distinct-count state. The classification transfers to no-repeat, at-most-k-frequency, and bounded-category windows.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_events: Sorting changes which events were adjacent in the original log, so it changes the candidate ranges.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_three: Three limits distinct types, not run length; a valid run may be much longer than three events.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_total: Distinctness is not derivable from one additive total of identifiers; frequencies or equivalent last-position state are required.

items.prompt: All values and target T are strictly positive. The goal is the shortest nonempty contiguous range whose sum is at least T. Why is a variable sliding window a legal candidate?
constraints: Every value is greater than zero.
T is greater than zero.
Only nonempty ranges are candidates.
The objective is minimum length with sum at least T.

options.text: Expanding cannot decrease the sum, and removing the leftmost positive value cannot increase it, so validity changes monotonically with each boundary move.
Any shortest-range problem uses a sliding window.
Positive values make the array effectively sorted.
Additivity alone is sufficient, even if values may be negative.

feedback.reason: Strict positivity gives the monotone sum behaviour needed to expand until valid and then shrink while valid.

blocks.text: For a fixed left boundary, moving right forward only increases the sum. Once the sum reaches T, moving left forward only decreases it, so each removal tests a strictly shorter candidate and eventually makes the window invalid. That monotonicity justifies never moving either pointer backward. The word ‘shortest’ is not sufficient, and additivity without sign restrictions does not guarantee the same boundary behaviour. Nonnegative values, including zero, preserve the non-decreasing/non-increasing property, although zeros may produce equal sums across moves.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.shortest_keyword: Shortest paths, edit problems, and many other minimum objectives are not sliding-window problems; the monotone repair rule is the decisive property.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.positive_means_sorted: Positive values say nothing about value order. They control how the sum changes when boundaries move.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sum_is_additive_only: With negative values, expansion can reduce the sum and removing the leftmost value can increase it, invalidating the simple shrink rule.

items.prompt: An array may contain positive and negative integers. Count all nonempty contiguous ranges whose sum is exactly T. Which strategy signal is decisive?
constraints: Values may have either sign.
Only nonempty ranges are counted.
Every qualifying range must be counted, not only a longest or shortest one.

options.text: Expand while the sum is below T and shrink while it is above T.
Use a fixed window of length T.
Use prefix sums with a frequency map: a range ending at r has sum T when an earlier prefix equals currentPrefix − T.
Sort the values and then apply a window.

feedback.reason: Exact-sum counting with mixed signs lacks a monotone repair rule; prefix-difference frequency preserves all possible starting boundaries.

blocks.text: Contiguity alone does not make a problem a sliding window. With signed values, adding or removing a value may raise or lower the sum, so a comparison with T cannot safely discard one left boundary. Define `prefix[j]` as the sum before position `j`; then the nonempty range `[l, r]` has sum `prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]`. It equals T exactly when the earlier prefix is `prefix[r+1] - T`.

items: Initialize the frequency map with prefix sum 0 occurring once, representing the boundary before the array.
Scan left to right and add the current value to `currentPrefix`.
Add `frequency[currentPrefix - T]` to the answer; every such earlier boundary starts a distinct qualifying nonempty range ending here.
Only after counting, increment `frequency[currentPrefix]`, so the current boundary cannot pair with itself as an empty range.

blocks.title: Signed trace
blocks.text: For `[1,-1,1]` and T=1, current prefixes are 1, 0, 1. The needed earlier prefixes are 0, -1, 0, contributing 1 + 0 + 2 = 3 ranges: `[0,0]`, `[0,2]`, and `[2,2]`.

blocks.title: When a simple window returns
blocks.text: A simple expand/shrink rule needs an additional monotone boundary, such as nonnegative values for an at-least threshold objective. Exact-sum counting with mixed signs has no such rule.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.simple_variable_window: The comparison with T does not tell which boundary move is safe when signs are mixed, so shrinking can discard a start that becomes valid later.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_window_t: T is a target sum, not a range length; qualifying ranges can have different sizes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_then_window: Sorting destroys original contiguity and therefore changes which ranges are legal.

items.prompt: Which combination is the strongest general signal for a sliding-window candidate?

options.text: A contiguous [left,right] candidate, state updated as boundaries move, and a predicate or fixed-size rule that supports safe movement.
Exactly two index variables, regardless of what the interval means.
Sorted input, even when the answer may choose nonadjacent values.
A hash map must appear in the implementation for the pattern to apply.

feedback.reason: The family is defined by contiguous-range state and a boundary update proof, not by syntax or one data structure.

blocks.text: A fixed window has a known width; a variable window has a validity predicate and a legal shrink rule. Both maintain one interval. Two indices, sortedness, and hash-map usage can occur in unrelated algorithms and are insufficient classification signals.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_indices_anywhere: Two indices can represent pairs, read/write compaction, or other state relations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_values: Sortedness supports pair elimination but does not imply contiguity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_map_required: Window state can be a scalar, counter, deque, or another structure.

items.prompt: A task asks for an aggregate over every consecutive block of exactly k input positions. Which recognition statement is correct?

options.text: It is a fixed-size sliding-window candidate; the left boundary advances once the right boundary creates a complete block.
It is a two-sum pair task because two boundaries appear in the notation.
It must be subsequence DP because every input position is considered.
It must shrink while a validity predicate fails, even though the width is fixed.

feedback.reason: Exact contiguity and fixed width determine the window state and update rule.

blocks.text: Maintain the aggregate for the last k positions by adding the incoming value and removing the value that falls out. No pair-elimination proof or variable validity repair is required. Negative values do not invalidate this exact-length invariant.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary_pair: The output contains every position in one consecutive block, not two arbitrary endpoints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.subsequence_dp: The task's interval aggregate has a direct rolling-state solution; considering each position does not imply subsequence choice.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_shrink: The width is prescribed, so a while-loop validity repair changes the output shape.

items.prompt: An array may contain signed values and the task counts all subarrays with sum exactly T. Which signal should prevent a naive expand-and-shrink window?

options.text: The current sum does not determine a safe boundary direction; prefix-sum state is a stronger candidate signal.
Contiguity alone guarantees a sliding window regardless of value signs.
Two boundaries prove that shrinking left preserves all future exact sums.
Negative values affect only performance, not correctness of the shrink rule.

feedback.reason: Exact signed sums lack the monotone relation needed to decide which starts can be discarded by one boundary move.

blocks.text: A prefix-sum map can count equal differences without assuming sign. A naive window may remove a negative and increase the sum or discard an earlier start that a future negative would make useful. Contiguity defines the answer shape, not the legality of every expand/shrink rule.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.contiguous_means_window: A contiguous target can require prefix sums or another strategy when validity is nonmonotone.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_indices_prove: Index syntax contains no discarded-candidate theorem.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_ignored: Signs can change the direction and outcome of each boundary update.

items.prompt: Select all statements that correctly distinguish fixed-size and variable-size sliding windows.

options.text: A fixed-size window removes the element k positions behind when a new element enters.
A variable-size window expands and shrinks according to a validity predicate or objective boundary.
Fixed-size windows require positive values for their rolling update to be correct.
Any variable window is correct as long as left eventually reaches right.

feedback.reason: Fixed width supplies the outgoing position directly; variable width needs a proof that its shrink rule preserves the objective.

blocks.text: A fixed window can maintain sums or other aggregates for arbitrary values because membership changes predictably. A variable window's while condition must be tied to validity and discarded-start safety; termination alone is not correctness. The distinction is the state contract, not the sign of values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_requires_positive: Fixed membership updates work with negative values as well.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_any_shrink: A terminating shrink may still skip valid or optimal ranges without a monotonicity proof.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_width: The exact width determines which element exits.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.variable_predicate: Variable movement needs a validity or objective condition to justify shrinkage.

items.prompt: Which wording most strongly signals a sliding-window representation?
constraints: The answer is based on a contiguous segment of an ordered input.
The segment can move as endpoints change.

options.text: Find the longest or shortest contiguous subarray/substring satisfying a condition.
options.explanation: The output geometry is exactly an interval of indices.

options.text: Choose any subset of elements regardless of their positions.
options.explanation: A subset may contain gaps and is not one window.

options.text: Evaluate every pair of positions with no contiguity requirement.
options.explanation: Pair search has a different state geometry.

options.text: Return a connected subtree of a rooted tree.
options.explanation: Tree topology is not a one-dimensional sliding interval.

feedback.reason: The strongest signal is a contiguous range whose endpoints can advance through the input.

blocks.text: Sliding-window state compresses the current interval and updates it as the left and right boundaries move. The input order and contiguity requirement are essential.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary_subset: A subset may contain gaps and is not one window.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_pairs: Pair search has a different state geometry.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_subtree: Tree topology is not a one-dimensional sliding interval.

items.prompt: Which contract distinguishes a fixed-size window from a general variable-size window?
constraints: Every output range has the same length k.
Adjacent outputs may overlap.

options.text: The right boundary advances one step while the left boundary advances one step per shift after the first k items.
The left boundary moves only when a validity predicate fails.
options.explanation: That is a variable-size repair rule.

options.text: Each next range starts after the previous range ends.
The input must be sorted so fixed length is well-defined.
options.explanation: Length is independent of value order.

feedback.reason: Fixed length determines a deterministic one-in/one-out transition after initialization.

blocks.text: A fixed-size scan does not use validity repair to choose its length. It emits each start position and maintains exactly k active elements, including overlaps.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.shrink_on_invalid: That is a variable-size repair rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_before_scan: Length is independent of value order.

items.prompt: When should prefix sums be considered before a sliding window for a contiguous range-sum query?
constraints: Array values may be negative.
The query asks for exact target sums or many arbitrary ranges.

options.text: Use prefix sums or a prefix-hash method when range sums are not monotone under endpoint movement or when arbitrary repeated range queries dominate.
options.explanation: Sliding shrink proofs need stronger monotonicity than prefix lookup does.

options.text: Any contiguous sum problem is best represented by a sliding window.
options.explanation: Negative values and arbitrary queries break the usual window advantages.

options.text: Sort values first so the window sum becomes monotone.
Prefix sums cannot answer a range query because they store only cumulative values.
options.explanation: Subtracting two prefixes is the standard exact range-sum query.

feedback.reason: The choice depends on value monotonicity and query shape, not merely on the word contiguous.

blocks.text: Positive values with a threshold often permit an amortized window. Signed values or many arbitrary exact queries favor prefix sums or prefix-plus-hash state because endpoint movement need not be monotone.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_window: Negative values and arbitrary queries break the usual window advantages.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_never: Subtracting two prefixes is the standard exact range-sum query.

items.prompt: A substring problem asks for the longest range with at most k distinct symbols. Which structural signal supports a variable-size window?
constraints: Adding a symbol can increase the distinct count.
Removing the leftmost symbol can decrease it.

options.text: The violation can be repaired by advancing left while the right boundary only moves forward, enabling an amortized linear scan.
options.explanation: This is the monotone validity structure.

options.text: The window is valid only when the distinct count equals k, so no shrink loop is needed.
options.explanation: At-most constraints require repair from counts above k.

options.text: Sort the symbols so distinctness becomes a fixed property of the entire input.
The key requirement is that all symbol values be positive.
options.explanation: Distinct-count windows depend on membership, not numeric positivity.

feedback.reason: At-most constraints with reversible membership state often give a monotone shrink condition.

blocks.text: A frequency map tracks the current window, and once distinct count exceeds k, moving left eventually restores validity. Because each pointer advances only forward, the total work is linear.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.exact_k_only: At-most constraints require repair from counts above k.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_sum: Distinct-count windows depend on membership, not numeric positivity.
